name: AI and Authorship
title: AI and Authorship
answer: AI and authorship concerns who or what can be credited as an author when artificial intelligence contributes to research writing, data analysis, or idea generation. It covers human accountability, disclosure of AI assistance, and the boundary between tool use and intellectual contribution. The topic sits within research integrity because authorship is tied to responsibility for the work. It also touches copyright and credit norms across journals and disciplines.

sections.body: AI and authorship concerns who or what can be credited as an author when artificial intelligence contributes to research writing, data analysis, or idea generation. It covers human accountability, disclosure of AI assistance, and the boundary between tool use and intellectual contribution. The topic sits within research integrity because authorship is tied to responsibility for the work. It also touches copyright and credit norms across journals and disciplines.
sections.heading: Scope

sections.body: The work runs on the same scholarly infrastructure as other research integrity questions: preprint servers, peer review systems, journal submission platforms, and institutional repositories. AI authorship discussions draw on large language models and other generative tools, but the governance layer is mostly human policy, editorial guidelines, and metadata standards. No special hardware is required beyond access to the models and the publication systems that record author lists.
sections.heading: What it runs on

sections.body: How the work is done involves close reading of journal policies, case studies of disputed authorship, and analysis of how researchers describe AI use in methods or acknowledgements. Some studies compare text produced with and without AI assistance to detect undisclosed use. Others survey editors, authors, and reviewers about their expectations. The core method is qualitative and policy oriented rather than a machine learning pipeline.
sections.heading: How the work is done

sections.body: Rights and risk and provenance center on the fact that AI systems cannot be authors under most current journal and publisher rules because they cannot take responsibility or transfer copyright. Risks include ghost authorship, undisclosed AI writing, erosion of accountability, and inflated author lists. Provenance questions ask who contributed what, whether AI output is traceable, and how to record assistance without granting authorship. Many publishers require disclosure of AI use in the methods or acknowledgements rather than the byline.
sections.heading: Rights, risk and provenance

sections.body: Where it is going is toward clearer, more granular disclosure standards and possibly machine readable contribution statements. Publishers and funders are likely to converge on common language for AI assistance, while tools for detecting AI text will remain contested. The bigger shift may be from asking whether AI can be an author to asking what authorship means when routine drafting, translation, and summarization are automated. Expect continued tension between efficiency and the human accountability that authorship exists to protect.
